header.name: Parallel Runtimes for Modern Processors (https://hipec.github.io/courses/cse513.html)
header.description: Computing hardware is becoming more and more complex. Today and in the foreseeable future, performance will be delivered principally by increased hardware parallelism. Modern multicore processors scale to over one hundred cores, have wide vector units, maintain a complex memory hierarchy and even share the memory with accelerators such as GPU. Conventional programming models using threads impose significant complexity to organize code into multiple threads of control and balance work amongst threads to ensure proper utilization of computing resources. This shortcoming has helped the advent of parallel runtimes that assist the programmer by efficiently scheduling the parallel tasks over available resources. This course introduces the design and implementation of such a parallel runtime and explores the challenges in achieving performance and energy efficiency over modern processors.
prerequisites_mandatory: Advanced Programming (CSE201), or any other programming intensive course

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Students develop insights on parallel programming abstractions and their corresponding hardware and software implementations

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Students have the ability to design and implement a low-overhead load balancing runtime for modern processors

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Students have the ability to implement runtime solutions for improving the performance of a parallel application over a modern processor

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Students develop insights on runtime techniques to improve the energy efficiency of a parallel application over a modern processor

lecture_topics: Introduction to modern processors: Multicore, vector units, GPUs, bandwidth and latency
Parallel programming on modern processors: Introduction to a modern lightweight low-level threading framework
Task parallellism and work-stealing runtime
SIMD parallelism using vectorization
runtime techniques for extracting SIMD parallelism from recursive task-parallel programs
hardware performance counters
Optimizing task parallel runtimes: techniques for controlling task granularity
scalable datastructures for task storage
assigning priorities to tasks
trace and replay of tasks in iterative parallel applications
Effect of caches and shared memory: cache coherency protocols
memory consistency
runtime techniques for detecting and avoiding false sharing
Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA)
programming models and runtimes for improving locality on a NUMA machine
Resilency: efficiently supporting resiliency in runtime systems
Energy efficient runtimes: Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS)
power capping
dynamically concurrency throttling
Advanced optimizations: Applying maching learning techniques in parallel runtimes
Implementing synchronization: data race detection (using vector clocks, etc.)
phasers
Heterogeneous runtime: unified runtime for hybrid CPU-GPU parallelism
automatic task partitioning across multicore CPU-GPU
Student seminars
